name: AIRC-LABWSN: A synchronized multimodal node-level time-series dataset for cross-layer anomaly detection in wireless sensor networks
description: AIRC-LABWSN is a multi-modal time series dataset at the node level, created to facilitate research on anomaly detection and inter-layer analysis in wireless sensor networks for smart agricultural applications. The dataset integrates environmental data from the Artichoke farming region in Da Lat, together with temporally and spatially expanded environmental data, topological information, and network data produced by packet-level ns-3 simulation. The data generation method has two phases: Phase 1 processes environmental measurements, including air temperature, air humidity, soil temperature, soil humidity, pH, electrical conductivity, and light intensity. The data augmentation model incorporates seasonal elements, diurnal variations, short-term meteorological changes, node discrepancies, and sensor interference. This step concurrently establishes a simulated topology including 40 sensor nodes and one sink/base station within a 100 m × 100 m region. Phase 2 uses the environmental data, network topology, and predefined event configuration as inputs for packet-level simulation in ns-3. The nodes are configured using IEEE 802.15.4 Low Rate Wireless Personal Area Network (LR-WPAN), 6LoWPAN, Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6), and User Datagram Protocol (UDP). In normal operational settings, each sensor node produces a UDP packet every five minutes when environmental input is available and relays it to the sink across a multi-hop pathway. Routing is implemented using an RPL-inspired parent-selection mechanism, with the resulting parent-child structure used to support multi-hop packet forwarding toward the sink. Throughout the simulation procedure, network measurements are consolidated in five-minute intervals and exported into network tables. Packet-generation, forwarding, link, queue, routing, sink-reception, and energy information is retained through intermediate records to support verification of the aggregated outputs. Node-level dynamic tables are linked using the key `(run_id, interval_id, node_id)`, while the link table additionally incorporates `neighbor_id`. The corresponding timestamp is retained as the human-readable UTC time coordinate. Rows impacted by network events are designated using the fields `is_anomaly`, `anomaly_type`, `anomaly_label`, and `primary_scenario_event_id`. The latter links affected observations to the corresponding event recorded in `scenario_events.csv`, while `observation_event_map.csv` provides additional event-to-observation provenance. The network data in AIRC-LABWSN represents inter-layer data produced via packet-level multi-hop ns-3 simulations, rather than data obtained directly from a physical network, including 41 nodes. The released dataset therefore combines real-world environmental observations with augmented environmental data and simulation-derived network measurements, while preserving supporting records for routing, packet delivery, and event provenance.

description: The Apnea-ECG Database is a foundational physiological signal benchmark developed for the Computers in Cardiology Challenge 2000 and hosted on PhysioNet. Contributed by Philipps University Marburg in Germany, the collection contains 70 overnight single-lead ECG recordings (approx 7 to 10 hours each) digitized at 100 Hz. name: ASLAD-190K: Arabic Sign Language Alphabet Dataset consisting of 190,000 Images
description: The ASLAD-190K dataset is an extensive collection containing 190,000 meticulously labeled RGB images representing 32 alphabets of the ArSL. To capture these images, we enlisted the help of two signers and utilized two different computer webcams, namely the HP HD camera and HP Truevision HD. The MediaPipe library was crucial in capturing RGB photos of various sizes. During the data collection process, we took great care to introduce diversity into the images. This involved varying lighting conditions, distances (zoom in/out), timings (day and night), 2D and 3D image rotations, and backgrounds. As a result, the dataset now offers a significantly augmented image corpus that closely resembles real-world scenarios, encompassing increasingly intricate situations. This augmentation enhances the performance of classification models during training. **How to cite** If you use ASLAD-190K in your research, please cite the following article: Boulesnane, A., Bellil, L. & Ghiri, M.G. name: Bangla Social Media Comments on the July 2024 Uprising in Bangladesh
description: This dataset contains 10,432 Bangla comments from public Facebook posts and YouTube videos about the July 2024 uprising in Bangladesh, each labelled Positive (6,076; 58.2%), Neutral (2,321; 22.2%) or Negative (2,035; 19.5%). The comments were scraped in 2025 from highly viewed posts and videos (about 20,000 collected), filtered for spam, bots and off-topic content, and then annotated by two final-year CSE students from the DIU NLP & ML Research Lab. A professor from the CSE department checked and corrected the labels. The labels reflect stance toward the movement as well as tone, and inter-annotator agreement was not computed. The CSV has two columns, `Text` (raw Bangla with emoji and punctuation preserved) and `Label`, with a median length of 9 words. It includes no usernames, links, timestamps or other metadata. Because slogans recur often, users should deduplicate and keep near-duplicate comments in one split before training. Oversampling before splitting inflated TF-IDF accuracy from 0.854 to 0.946 in our experiments. Under a leakage-controlled protocol, BanglaBERT (BUET) reaches a macro-F1 of 0.867, while a few-shot Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct reaches 0.616. The dataset is intended for Bangla sentiment analysis, political discourse research and leakage-aware benchmarking. The comments come from popular public posts on two platforms and are dominated by Positive sentiment, so results describe this corpus and not Bangladeshi public opinion. Comments deleted before 2025 are missing. Only public comments are included, but short ones can still be found by searching the platforms, so users must not attempt to re-identify authors or use the data for profiling.

name: BanglaAuth-12: A Bangla Literary Text Dataset for Authorship Identification and Attribution
description: BanglaAuth-12 is a Bangla literary text dataset developed to support research on authorship identification, authorship attribution, natural language processing (NLP), and text classification. The dataset was collected from September to December 2024 by students of the DIU NLP & ML Research Lab at Daffodil International University (DIU), Bangladesh, under the supervision of the Lab Supervisor. The dataset contains 4,105 records, primarily comprising Bangla literary text passages associated with author names and book titles. The source material includes literary works by notable Bangla-language writers, including Jibanananda Das, Rabindranath Tagore, Kazi Nazrul Islam, Humayun Ahmed, Satyajit Ray, Manik Bandopadhyay, Muhammad Zafar Iqbal, Abul Asad, and Sukumar Ray. The current CSV contains 12 distinct author-label strings before normalization; whitespace normalization reduces this to 10 distinct labels, with a remaining spelling variation for Sukumar Ray that requires standardization. Each record primarily contains three fields: the text passage (`Para`), the corresponding author label (`Author Name`), and the associated book title (`Book`). The dataset includes both prose and poetry passages, making it potentially useful for studying stylistic differences across authors and literary texts. Potential applications include supervised authorship classification, stylometric analysis, Bangla text representation learning, feature engineering, machine-learning and deep-learning model evaluation, and comparative experiments involving traditional text-classification methods and transformer-based language models. The dataset is distributed in CSV format for convenient use with Python, pandas, and common NLP and machine-learning frameworks. Researchers should inspect missing values, standardize author-name variants, verify text-to-author mappings, and establish appropriate training and testing splits before conducting experiments. Where multiple passages originate from the same book or source, evaluation should account for potential source leakage. This dataset is intended to facilitate research on Bangla-language computational linguistics and authorship analysis. Researchers should verify the provenance, licensing, and applicable reuse permissions of the underlying literary texts before redistribution or commercial use.

name: BanglaCineAspect: A dataset for aspect-based sentiment analysis of Bangla movie reviews
description: BanglaCineAspect is a dataset of 1,421 Bangla movie reviews annotated for aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA). Each review is labelled for nine aspects of a film: Direction, Acting, Songs & Music, Screenplay, Story, Cinematography, Background Music, Editing and Dialogue. An aspect is coded 1 if the review expresses a positive opinion about it, 0 if the opinion is negative, and left blank if the review does not mention it. The dataset contains 3,786 aspect labels (2,696 positive and 1,090 negative), with 2.66 aspects per review on average. Reviews were collected from five sources: a Google Form shared with Bangla-speaking viewers, reviews gathered in person, YouTube comments, and user reviews on IMDb and Letterboxd. Every review comes with English text. Two annotators labelled the reviews, and 100 reviews were labelled by both to measure agreement (Cohen's kappa = 0.775; observed agreement = 88.56%). The repository contains two archives: 1. RawDataset.zip: the reviews and labels as originally collected and annotated (1,428 rows), before any cleaning. 2. BanglaCineAspect_preprocessed_dataset.zip: the cleaned dataset used for modelling, containing: - Bangla_Movie_Reviews_ABSA_preprocessed.csv and .xlsx: 1,421 reviews with 14 columns (review_id, review_bn_clean, review_bn_original, review_en, source_excel_row and the nine aspect columns). The CSV is UTF-8 with BOM so Bangla displays correctly in Excel. - data_dictionary.csv: description of every column and of the label coding. - dropped_rows.csv: the 7 exact-duplicate rows removed during cleaning, with their original row numbers. - README.txt: a short summary of the dataset and cleaning steps. The data can be used to train and evaluate aspect-level sentiment classifiers for Bangla, to compare deep learning and transformer models on a low-resource language, and to study cross-lingual sentiment analysis using the parallel English text.

name: BanglaClauseBench: A clause-level annotated dataset of Bangla sentences
description: BanglaClauseBench is a hand-annotated dataset for clause-level analysis of Bangla (Bengali). It contains 9,062 sentences, 24,475 clauses and 132,242 tokens. We collected the text from public Facebook posts, online Bangla news portals, blogs and YouTube comments. We removed usernames, profile links, URLs, timestamps and anything else that could identify a person. Every token has a Universal POS tag. For every clause we record: clause_text: the clause as it appears in the sentence clause_type: MAIN, COORDINATE, COMPLEMENT, SUBORDINATE, CONDITIONAL, RELATIVE or TEMPORAL head_verb: the predicate head, including multi-word complex predicates subject and object: if the subject is dropped, the annotators wrote the subject they understood from context connector: the word or suffix that links the clause, e.g. যদি, যে, এবং, -লে dependency_relation: root, conj, advcl, ccomp, relcl, xcomp or acl parent_clause: the clause it depends on Together, these fields turn each sentence into a small clause tree. Three annotators labelled every sentence on their own. We kept a label when at least two agreed, and a fourth expert decided when all three differed. Mean pairwise Cohen's kappa is 0.87.

name: BanglaDial-4D: A Four-District Bangla Speech Corpus for Dialect Identification and Recording-Channel Robustness Research
description: BanglaDial-4D is a Bangla speech corpus developed for research on regional dialect identification, acoustic analysis, and the robustness of speech classification systems to speaker and recording-channel variations. The dataset contains 2,557 cleaned audio recordings collected from native Bangla speakers associated with four districts of Bangladesh: Dhaka, Chittagong, Noakhali, and Bogura. These locations represent central, south-eastern, and northern regional varieties of Bangla. The corpus was collected in 2025 by students of the DIU NLP and ML Research Lab. It initially contained 2,696 audio files, from which 139 files were removed during cleaning, including duplicate recordings. The final corpus comprises approximately 4.82 hours of total audio and 4.05 hours of speech. Twenty-four native speakers participated in the collection, including 8 speakers from Dhaka, 8 from Chittagong, 6 from Noakhali, and 2 from Bogura. Participants were aged 18–23; 15 were male and 9 were female. Speakers read scripted material and recorded themselves at home using their own mobile phones. The recordings retain variation in file formats, codecs, sample rates, recording applications, and acoustic conditions. These characteristics make the corpus useful not only for dialect classification but also for investigating potential confounding factors in speech machine learning. In particular, researchers can examine whether a model learns regional linguistic characteristics or instead relies on speaker identity, recording devices, file metadata, compression artifacts, or background noise. Each recording is associated with a district-level label and available file-level metadata. The dataset is intended for research involving acoustic and prosodic feature extraction, classical machine learning, deep neural networks, self-supervised speech representations, robustness testing, and confound-aware evaluation. It may also support investigations into data leakage and the reliability of reported performance in regional speech classification. Important limitations: The corpus contains relatively few speakers, with only two speakers represented for Bogura. The original file-to-speaker mapping was not recorded; estimated speaker-and-device clusters were therefore used in the associated study. These clusters should not be treated as verified speaker identities. Recording sources also differ across districts, so the corpus does not support an assumption that dialect and recording conditions are independent. Results obtained from this dataset should be interpreted with these limitations in mind. All participants provided informed consent before recording. Public redistribution of the audio should be undertaken only in accordance with the scope of that consent and any applicable institutional requirements.

name: BanglaGender-10K: A Labeled Bangla Text Dataset for Gender Classification and Gender-Conditioned Text Generation
description: BanglaGender-10K is a Bangla-language text dataset designed to support research in natural language processing (NLP), text classification, and gender-conditioned text generation. The dataset was collected in 2025 as an extension of an earlier Bangla literary text collection developed in 2024. The dataset contains 10,100 Bangla text samples organized into two gender-associated categories: Male and Female. It is provided in CSV format with two columns: `Text`, which contains the Bangla textual content, and `Gender`, which provides the corresponding class label. The dataset includes 5,100 Male-labeled samples and 5,000 Female-labeled samples, providing a near-balanced distribution for binary classification experiments. Total 20 authors used in this dataset: 10 Male & 10 Female. The primary objective of the dataset is to facilitate the development and evaluation of computational methods for distinguishing between the two provided text-label categories. Potential applications include supervised text classification, linguistic feature analysis, text representation learning, gender-conditioned text generation, and exploratory research on gender-associated patterns in Bangla text. The dataset may also serve as a starting point for investigating text-style transformation between Male and Female target categories. However, direct Male-to-Female or Female-to-Male transformation requires an appropriate generation framework and evaluation methodology; the dataset does not itself establish that corresponding texts are parallel or provide paired transformation examples. Researchers can use the dataset to investigate traditional machine-learning classifiers, deep-learning architectures, and transformer-based language models for Bangla text processing. Recommended evaluation procedures include stratified train-validation-test splits, macro-averaged F1-score, precision, recall, and confusion-matrix analysis. Duplicate-text checks and leakage-aware splitting should be considered before model training. The dataset is intended to support reproducible research in Bangla NLP and gender-associated text analysis. The Male and Female labels should be interpreted as the categories provided in the dataset rather than as definitive evidence of an author's gender or of universal linguistic characteristics associated with gender. Researchers should review the dataset's collection and labeling procedures before drawing broader conclusions. name: BanglaHand: A Dataset of Handwritten Paragraphs for Writer-Independent Handedness Recognition
description: BanglaHand is a benchmark dataset of 42 writers (21 naturally left-handed and 21 right-handed) designed for offline handwriting analysis and handedness recognition in Bangla script. It contains 336 high-resolution smartphone photographs of complete handwritten paragraphs captured under rigorously controlled conditions. Key Highlights: • Balanced Demographic Benchmark: 21 confirmed left-handed and 21 right-handed writers, providing a 1:1 balanced distribution in a population where left-handed writing is exceptionally rare (approx. 1–2%). • Dual-Condition Text Design: Each writer contributed 8 paragraphs: - 6 shared prompts (S01–S06, 49–54 words each) identical across all writers for content-controlled benchmarking. - 2 writer-specific paragraphs on self-chosen topics to test generalization to unseen text. • Controlled Materials & Capture: All participants wrote using pens and paper from a single common supply in mixed writing sessions. All pages were photographed in one session with a Samsung Galaxy A17 smartphone (4080 × 2296 pixels) in mixed order. • Geometric Audit & Quality Control: A SIFT + RANSAC homography screening across all writer pairs confirmed writer uniqueness and prevented page duplicates. Images were rotated upright (lossless 4:4:4 JPEG, quality 98) without cropping, resizing, or photometric filtering. name: BanglaHateLens-3D: A three-dimensional Bengali hate speech dataset with type, severity and target annotations
description: BanglaHateLens-3D is a comprehensive, structured Bengali-language hate speech dataset comprising 50,746 annotated comments, designed to support research in natural language processing (NLP), hate speech detection, offensive language analysis, and multidimensional text classification. The dataset incorporates three complementary annotation dimensions: Type of Hate, Severity of Hate, and Target of Hate, enabling systematic analysis of harmful language, its intensity, and its intended targets. The dataset includes six hate-type classes (None, Abusive, Political Hate, Profane, Religious Hate, and Sexism), three severity levels (Little to None, Mild, and Severe), and five target classes (None, Individual, Organization, Community, and Society). Furthermore, the comments are organized into 19 topical categories and 120 subcategories, facilitating detailed analysis of linguistic patterns and harmful discourse across diverse contexts. BanglaHateLens-3D consists of 35,522 training instances, 5,024 development instances, and 10,200 testing instances. The dataset is provided in UTF-8 encoded JSON and CSV formats, ensuring accessibility and compatibility with conventional machine learning algorithms, deep learning architectures, and transformer-based language models. The repository is organized into two components: (1) Dataset, containing annotated Bengali comments and predefined training, development, and testing partitions; (2) Metadata & Others Validation Data, providing comprehensive documentation, data dictionaries, annotation specifications, class distribution statistics, structural validation reports, duplicate analysis, and SHA-256 checksum verification. To support data quality and reproducibility, the repository includes validation resources for assessing dataset structure, annotation consistency, data completeness, and file integrity. The structured organization and accompanying documentation facilitate transparent experimental workflows, systematic evaluation, and comparative benchmarking. BanglaHateLens-3D serves as a valuable resource for advancing Bengali-language hate speech research, particularly in low-resource NLP, multidimensional classification, severity assessment, target identification, automated content moderation, and responsible artificial intelligence. Its multidimensional annotation framework supports the development and evaluation of robust computational models for identifying and analyzing harmful online communication.

description: BanglaSentiNet is a corpus of 28,000 Bangla text records jointly annotated for fine-grained sentiment polarity and emotion. name: BD-AgroMet56
description: BD-AgroMet56 is a division-level time-series dataset that links crop statistics with meteorological records for Bangladesh from 1970 to 2025. It covers six major crops (Aus rice, Aman rice, Boro rice, Wheat, Potato and Jute) across the eight administrative divisions, giving 2,688 annual records and 22 variables. Each record combines crop production, cultivated area and yield with growing-season climate variables, including temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind speed, sunshine, solar radiation and evapotranspiration. Crop data were compiled from the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) and climate data from the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD). Climate values come from one BMD station per division, so they represent station conditions rather than dense spatial coverage within a division. Crop records were harmonized to the current eight-division structure, and the data were checked for duplicates, missing values, non-positive values, temporal coverage and yield consistency. Some sunshine, evapotranspiration and solar radiation values are missing in the source and were left unaltered. The dataset supports analysis of long-term yield trends, division-level comparisons and relationships between climate and crop yield.

name: Behavioral and Neural Measures of Auditory Distraction in Participants with Tinnitus
description: In this exploratory study, we tested whether tinnitus burden, assessed using the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI), was associated with behavioral and neural responses to external auditory distraction. Thirty adults with chronic tinnitus completed behavioral and electroencephalographic (EEG) testing. Participants with lower and higher THI scores were similar in age and hearing thresholds. Data from twenty-three neurotypical adults provided an additional reference cohort. Participants classified sequences of amplitude-modulated tones as random or repeating during behavioral testing or combined behavioral and EEG recording sessions. Competing noise or melodic distractors imposed lower and higher levels of distraction, respectively. Melodic distractors reduced response accuracy more than noise distractors, with comparable effects in the lower and higher THI groups. Neural synchronization to changes in the target sequence also de-creased more with melodic distractors, but this effect did not differ between groups. Other measures of synchronization to target and distractor features showed no significant group differences. Descriptions of data headers can be found in the included README document. Figure numbers refer to the manuscript reporting these results, available as a preprint at https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.01.27.702073

name: A Bilingual Deep Learning Framework for Real-World Afghan License Plate Detection and Persian–English Recognition
description: This dataset contains approximately 8,500 annotated images of vehicles and license plates from Afghanistan and was prepared for the development and evaluation of an automatic license plate detection system. The dataset focuses on the detection stage of an Automatic License Plate Recognition (ALPR) pipeline, where the objective is to identify and localize the license plate region within a full vehicle or scene image. Each image contains a vehicle or scene in which a license plate is visible. The license plate regions are annotated using bounding boxes that define the location of the plate within the image. These annotations enable object detection models to learn how to locate Afghan license plates within complete images before the recognition stage is performed. The dataset includes variations in vehicle type, license plate appearance, viewing angle, distance, background, illumination, and image quality. These variations provide realistic conditions for developing and evaluating license plate detection models. The dataset is organized into training, validation, and testing subsets to support model training and performance evaluation. The annotations are provided in COCO JSON format, which stores image information, object categories, and bounding-box coordinates in a structured format. This makes the dataset suitable for different object detection frameworks and allows the annotations to be converted into other formats when necessary. In our research, this dataset was used for the detection component of an end-to-end Afghan License Plate Recognition pipeline. A YOLO-based object detection model was trained to locate license plates within full images. Once a license plate is detected, its region can be cropped from the original image and passed to a separate Optical Character Recognition (OCR) model for character recognition. Therefore, this published dataset specifically represents the license plate detection component of the system and does not include the separate augmented dataset used for training the recognition model. The dataset can support research in automatic license plate detection, Automatic License Plate Recognition (ALPR), computer vision, intelligent transportation systems, traffic monitoring, and object detection. By making the dataset publicly available, it can support the reproducibility of the detection experiments and provide a resource for researchers interested in developing and evaluating computer vision approaches for Afghan license plates.

name: BnPostDuo
description: BnPostDuo is a paired-text dataset of 4,800 Bengali social media image posts for multi-class content classification. Each post has two text views: the caption the publisher wrote with the image, and the text embedded in the image, extracted by optical character recognition (OCR). The original images are not released because of copyright restrictions. Instead, each record keeps a 64-bit perceptual hash (pHash) and the image's original width and height, so records can be traced and checked for duplicates without sharing the images. The dataset has eight balanced categories with 600 posts each: Educational, Entertainment, Marketing, Motivational, News, Political, Religious and Social Awareness. Files: - Bengali_Multimodal_Dataset.csv: all 4,800 records (8 columns). - class_csvs/: eight per-category CSV files (600 records each), the same records without the label column. All files are UTF-8 encoded and have no missing values. Columns: - image_id: unique identifier (/.jpg) - caption: the caption that accompanied the post - raw_ocr: unedited OCR output, including watermarks, logos, dates and recognition noise - main_ocr: cleaned OCR text keeping the main message of the image - phash: 16-character hexadecimal perceptual hash of the source image - image_width, image_height: original image size in pixels - label: content category The text is mostly Bengali with some English mixed in, and includes emoji, URLs, hashtags and deliberately broken-up words, as they appeared in the original posts. Median length is 11 tokens for captions, 11 for cleaned OCR and 27 for raw OCR. Captions and image text are often different from each other, especially in the Marketing and Social Awareness categories, so the two views carry complementary information. The dataset can be used for Bengali text classification, caption-only vs. image-text vs. fused-input modelling, OCR post-correction (raw_ocr to main_ocr), noisy-text robustness studies, and benchmarking Bengali language models on social media content.

name: Bone Fracture and Non-Fracture Radiograph Dataset of Hand, Hip Joint and Leg from Bangladesh
description: This dataset contains 864 plain radiograph (X-ray) images labelled for bone fracture detection across three anatomical regions: the upper limb (hand and arm), the hip joint, and the lower limb (leg, ankle and foot). The images were collected between February and April 2025 from Satkhira, Bangladesh. Students of the DIU NLP & ML Research Lab, Daffodil International University, collected and labelled the data under the supervision of the lab's supervisors. The images are organised into six folders, one per class: Hand Fracture: 325 images Hand Non Fracture: 294 images Hip Joint Fracture: 240 images Hip Joint Non Fracture: 288 images Leg Fracture: 352 images Leg Non Fracture: 430 images Images are in JPG and PNG format, with resolutions from about 159 to 1,873 pixels per side. They were exported from the hospital imaging viewer and cropped to the region of interest, so some images keep a thin viewer border and side markers (LT/RT). All patient-identifying information was removed before release. The classes are imbalanced, especially in the hip joint category. Users should apply augmentation or class weighting inside the training split only, after splitting the data, to avoid data leakage. The dataset can be used for binary fracture detection, region-specific fracture classification, six-class classification, transfer learning, and testing deep learning models on radiographs from a low-resource clinical setting in South Asia.

description: CAMELYON16 is a landmark digital pathology benchmark for automated detection of metastases in whole-slide histopathology images (WSIs) of breast cancer sentinel lymph node sections. name: A Comprehensive Real-World Dataset of Jackfruit Leaf Diseases and Growth Stages for Intelligent Crop Health Monitoring
description: This study presents a high-quality dataset of jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus) leaf images collected using smartphone cameras from agricultural areas in Savar and Rajbari, Bangladesh. The dataset comprises 1,026 original images distributed across eight classes: Blight, Dried, Fungal Spot, Healthy, Leaf Miner, Pest Damage, Senescence, and Young. The original dataset was partitioned into training (70%), validation (15%), and testing (15%) subsets, containing 714, 162, and 150 images, respectively. To mitigate class imbalance and enhance visual diversity, data augmentation techniques, including horizontal flipping, random rotation, random cropping, zooming, and brightness adjustment, were applied exclusively to the training subset, producing 8,000 training images with 1,000 images per class. All images were resized to 512 × 512 pixels and stored in JPG format with RGB color representation. This dataset provides a resource for developing and evaluating machine learning and deep learning models for jackfruit leaf disease classification, leaf growth-stage recognition, and precision agriculture applications.

name: Deep Learning-Based Automated Identification of Bean and Gourd Crop Diseases.
description: This dataset contains 4,155 raw RGB images of bean and gourd crops (leaves and fruits) in 10 classes (6 disease and 4 healthy), prepared for automated plant disease classification research using deep learning. The labels of these images were assigned with the help of local farmers and an agriculture officer from Sherpur. One author of the source dataset is also an author of the present dataset. The final dataset was checked and organized by the authors. The authors did not add any augmented images. Dataset information: • Total images: 4,155 • Number of classes: 10 • Image type: RGB • Format: Raw images in class-specific folders (no train/validation/test split) Intended applications include plant disease classification, transfer learning, agricultural computer vision, and deep learning research. name: EEG-Based Lie Detection Dataset using 14-Channel Emotiv EPOC+: Instructed-Response and Free-Response Protocols
description: This dataset contains EEG recordings from 54 participants collected with a 14-channel Emotiv EPOC+ headset (128 Hz, EmotivPRO software) during a question-and-answer deception task. Two protocols are included: an instructed-response protocol (32 participants), where participants were told in advance whether to answer each question truthfully or deceptively, giving unambiguous experimenter-assigned labels; and a free-response protocol (22 participants), where participants freely chose and self-reported whether they lied or told the truth. Both protocols use the same 32-question set, split into four categories — Personal Information, General Knowledge, Control, and Situation-Based. Data is organized as Instructed_Response and Free_Response, each with one folder per de-identified participant (Subject1–Subject32, Subject1–Subject22), and within each participant folder, recordings are split into true and false subfolders per EmotivPRO's trial label. Each trial is stored as three files: a .json metadata file, a .md.mc.pm.fe.bp.csv file with the raw 14-channel EEG plus Emotiv's motion, facial-expression, mental-command, and band-power outputs, and an _intervalMarker.csv file. The instructed-response protocol has an even 512/512 truth/lie split; the free-response protocol's split varies by participant since labeling was self-reported. This study was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Independent University, Bangladesh (IUB) — Research Project Number 2025-SETS-NSR:04, "Design and Development of a Lie Detection System Using EEG Signals," approved September 4, 2025, under Principal Investigator Dr. Md. Kafiul Islam. Informed consent was obtained from all participants, who are identified in the dataset only by de-identified study IDs.

name: FabriD:Fabric Defect Detection Dataset
description: FabriD is a fabric defect detection and segmentation dataset comprising real-world fabric images designed to support research in computer vision, image classification, object detection, instance segmentation, and intelligent textile recognition. The dataset contains five image categories, including four fabric defect classes and one defect-free class: - Needle Mark: 467 images - Hole: 459 images - Stains: 407 images - Missing Yarn: 454 images - Defect-free: 620 images The dataset contains a total of 2,407 images. These images represent diverse visual conditions, including variations in illumination, viewing angles, fabric textures, wrinkles, folds, and background complexity. Such diversity makes the dataset suitable for developing and evaluating deep learning models for automated fabric inspection and defect analysis. The images were annotated manually using the Roboflow annotation platform to support image classification, object detection, and instance segmentation tasks. Depending on the annotation task, the dataset includes class labels, polygon annotations, and segmentation masks for defect localization and delineation. The annotations were manually reviewed to improve label consistency and reduce annotation errors. FabriD provides a resource for researchers and practitioners working on automated textile inspection and fabric defect analysis. Potential applications include quality control, smart manufacturing, textile production monitoring, and the development of intelligent fabric inspection systems. The dataset can also support comparative evaluations of computer vision and deep learning approaches for fabric defect detection and segmentation.

name: Grapevine Bunch Images with Powdery Mildew Severity Labels Collected under Field Conditions
description: This dataset comprises 2,068 field images of grapevine (Vitis vinifera L.) bunches with image-level labels describing four ordinal grades of visible powdery mildew severity: Healthy, Mild, Moderate, and Severe. It was developed to support computer vision research on plant disease severity classification under field conditions. Images were acquired during the 2023 fruiting season in a commercial vineyard in Bouarg, Nador Province, northeastern Morocco. Photographs were captured using a Sony α230 digital single-lens reflex camera equipped with an 18–55 mm lens. Images were recorded in JPEG format at a native resolution of 3872 × 2592 pixels. Bunches were photographed in situ under natural illumination, preserving the vineyard background and variations in lighting, viewing angle, berry appearance, and partial occlusion. Severity labels characterise the visible symptoms on the photographed bunch. Healthy denotes the absence of visible powdery mildew symptoms; Mild indicates limited, localised symptoms; Moderate represents more extensive but partial involvement; and Severe denotes widespread symptoms with pronounced visual alteration. These labels describe visible disease severity in the image rather than a laboratory-confirmed measure of infection. The annotation table links each image filename to its severity code through the image_id and global_degree fields, with codes 0, 1, 2, and 3 corresponding to Healthy, Mild, Moderate, and Severe, respectively. Additional fields provide a descriptive annotation comment and an exclusion indicator. Labels are assigned at the source-image level; they do not constitute pixel-level segmentation masks or independent annotations of individual image patches. Potential applications include supervised image classification, ordinal severity modelling, transfer learning, and the comparative evaluation of convolutional and Transformer-based models. When generating patches or augmented samples, users should partition the original images before deriving these samples, ensuring that samples originating from the same image remain within a single partition to prevent data leakage. As the dataset originates from one vineyard and one growing season, performance on other locations, cultivars, and acquisition conditions requires independent validation.

name: Hijaiyah Letter Pronunciation Audio Dataset for Articulation Characteristic Classification
description: This dataset contains audio recordings of Arabic (hijaiyah) letters pronounced correctly and incorrectly, collected to support research on automatic classification of letter pronunciation characteristics (sifat huruf) in Quranic recitation learning. Content - 21,600 WAV recordings, balanced between two classes: "Data Benar" (correct pronunciation, 10,800 files) and "Data Salah" (incorrect pronunciation, 10,800 files). - Each class has 20 numbered sub-folders; each sub-folder holds the recordings of one respondent (540 files per sub-folder). - Each respondent pronounced 36 items (the 28 hijaiyah letters plus letter variants), each with 3 vowel marks (harakat: 1 = fathah, 2 = kasrah, 3 = dhammah), repeated 5 times. - Recordings are mono, mostly 44.1 kHz (a few at 48 kHz), and about 0.7-1.0 seconds long. - File naming: --.wav, e.g. 21-1-1.wav = item 21, fathah, repetition 1. Annotation Each letter is annotated with 12 binary/ternary label variables covering 18 articulation characteristics (sifat huruf), following Al-Hafiz (2014). Five variables encode opposing pairs (S) and seven encode characteristics without an opposite (T): S1: jahr = 0 / hams = 1 S2: rakhawah = 0 / bayniyyah = 1 / syiddah = 2 S3: istifal = 0 / isti'la = 1 S4: infitah = 0 / ithbaq = 1 S5: ishmat = 0 / idzlaq = 1 T1 shafir, T2 qalqalah, T3 liin, T4 inhirah, T5 takrir, T6 tafasysyi, T7 istithaalah (1 = present, 0 = absent). Labels follow the letter and, for some letters, the vowel mark (e.g. tafkhim of some letters depends on the vowel). In the accompanying article, three properties are modelled: S1 (jahr-hams), S3 (tarqiq-tafkhim) and T2 (qalqalah). For the incorrect class, the label of these three properties is the inverse of the correct label of the same item. [Fill in: label convention for the incorrect class for the other nine properties, or state that they are given for the correct class only.] The documentation lists the exact rules, the 9 recordings with non-standard file names excluded from experiments (21,591 recordings used), and respondent sub-folders that contain identical recordings. Additional files - Label and index tables (one row per recording, with respondent and cross-validation group). - Respondent-level train/test split (seed 42) and 5-fold cross-validation assignment. - Source code for preprocessing (resampling, voice activity detection, noise reduction, trimming, normalisation), augmentation (time stretching, pitch shifting, additive noise, time shifting), feature extraction (MFCC, Mel spectrogram, LPC) and model training. Intended use Training and evaluating classifiers for letter pronunciation characteristics. Because several recordings per respondent exist, splits must be made at respondent level to avoid data leakage; augmented copies must follow the split of their source recording.

name: HSC-IndicDB: A Hierarchical Multi-Task Dataset for Isolated Character and Numeral Recognition Across Six Indic Scripts
description: The dataset contains isolated handwritten and paleographical character samples across six Indic writing systems (Devanagari, Sharada, Nandinagari, Malayalam, Bengali, and Kannada), spanning Northern Nagari and Southern Dravidian lineages. The data was gathered from digitized historical manuscript folios, archival paper documents, and standardized handwritten transcription forms contributed by a diverse cohort of scribes and writers across different age groups. The document folios underwent high-resolution scanning, automated isolated glyph extraction, bounding-box cropping, and adaptive Sauvola binarization to mitigate substrate degradation, ink bleed, and background artifacts. After manually inspecting the corpus and discarding fragmented strokes, obscured contours, and illegible scribbles, the finalized benchmark repository comprises 36,152 digitized glyph images. The entire collection is organized into a clean directory hierarchy, sorted systematically into respective parent folders corresponding to each script lineage and script type, and subdivided into individual subfolders labeled by character and numeral class.

name: INMAD (Indonesia - Madurese) Sentences Dataset
description: The INMAD (Indonesia-Madurese) Sentence Dataset is a trilingual parallel corpus containing sentences in English, Indonesian, and Madurese, designed to support the development of natural language processing (NLP) technology for low-resource languages. This dataset integrates three primary sources from the IndoNLP repository: Korpus Nusantara (1,100 sentences), NusaX MT (994 sentences), and Nusa Paragraf (9,449 sentences), yielding a combined total of 11,543 parallel sentence pairs consolidated into a single raw CSV file. To increase the variety and volume of the dataset, data augmentation was performed via back-translation using the MarianMT model in Python with translating Indonesian sentences into English and then back into Indonesian, effectively doubling the corpus to 23,086 parallel sentence pairs. All Madurese translations were produced manually at the engghi-enten speech register by expert translators to ensure linguistic quality and naturalness. The English translations, derived from the back-translation process, were retained as an additional language column to support multilingual NLP tasks. This version presents a revised and cleaned edition of the dataset. A multi-stage data cleaning process was applied to improve overall data quality. Sentences containing the following types of noise were identified and removed: (1) word abbreviations and informal shorthand that do not reflect natural language structure; (2) hyperlinks and URLs embedded within sentence text; (3) emoticons and emoji characters; (4) social media artifacts such as hashtags (#) and mentions (@); and (5) other non-linguistic elements that may negatively affect model training. This cleaning process was applied to both the Indonesian and Madurese columns to ensure consistency across language pairs. The final dataset consists of 23,086 parallel sentence entries stored in CSV format with UTF-8 encoding, organized into three columns: english, indonesia, and madurese (Madurese translation at the engghi-enten register). This dataset is intended for use in machine translation development, cross-lingual NLP research, language preservation efforts, and digital lexicography for the Madurese language.

name: Kvasir-Capsule: Video Capsule Endoscopy Dataset
description: Kvasir-Capsule is an open-access video capsule endoscopy (VCE) dataset collected by Simula Research Laboratory and Bærum Hospital in Norway, published in Nature Scientific Data. Providing unconstrained visual insights into the human small intestine, the dataset comprises 47,238 labeled bounding frames and 117 video sequences from capsule endoscopy examinations. Annotations span 14 distinct pathological and anatomical classes, including vascular lesions (angiectasia), inflammatory changes (ulcers, erosion, erythema), luminal blood, polypoid lesions, and standard anatomical markers (ileocecal valve, pylorus). Kvasir-Capsule enables computer vision researchers to develop automated abnormality detection algorithms that alleviate the labor-intensive burden of reviewing multi-hour capsule videos.

name: MedEquip30: A Multi-Device Dataset for Medical Equipment Detection
description: MedEquip30 is a real-world image dataset of 30 types of commonly used medical and first-aid equipment, such as blood pressure monitors, thermometers, glucometers, pulse oximeters, surgical instruments, and everyday consumables like gauze, bandages, and saline. The images were taken from several places using four smartphones: Apple iPhone 15 Pro, OnePlus 9R, Samsung Galaxy A56, and Samsung Galaxy A05s. Photos were captured under different lighting, backgrounds, and viewing angles to reflect real clinical settings. The dataset contains 4,504 images and 13,492 polygon annotations. All images are resized to 640 × 640 pixels and split into training (70%), validation (20%), and test (10%) sets. Annotations are provided in COCO JSON format, and a metadata file lists the subset, object classes, and capture device for each image. The dataset can be used for object detection, instance segmentation, and cross-device evaluation, and supports applications such as equipment inventory monitoring and readiness checking in healthcare facilities. Details of the collection process and benchmark results with YOLOv11 and RF-DETR are given in the related article.

name: MedSynthDetect: A Real vs AI-Generated Medical Image Dataset of X-ray, CT and MRI
description: This dataset is designed for detecting AI-generated (synthetic) medical images. It contains real and AI-generated images from three imaging modalities: X-ray, computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The real images were collected between February and April 2025 from publically available data source. The AI-generated images were created with ChatGPT using text prompts that ask for realistic medical scans of each modality. A student of the DIU NLP & ML Research Lab, Daffodil International University, prepared the dataset under the supervision of the lab's supervisors. The dataset is organised into six folders: X-ray: real X-ray images (500) AI_X-ray: ChatGPT-generated X-ray images (500) CT Scan: real CT images (500) AI_CT Scan: ChatGPT-generated CT images (500) MRI: real MRI images ([496]) AI_MRI: ChatGPT-generated MRI images ([385]) Images in each folder are numbered sequentially (1, 2, 3, …). All images were resized to 512×512 pixels and saved in PNG format, so that file format and resolution do not reveal whether an image is real or synthetic. Exact duplicate images were removed. All patient-identifying information was removed from the real images. The dataset supports binary real-vs-fake classification, six-class classification (modality × authenticity), cross-modality generalisation studies (for example, training on X-ray and testing on MRI), and benchmarking of deepfake and synthetic-image detectors in medical imaging. With generative AI tools now widely available, fabricated medical images are a risk to clinical trust, insurance and research integrity. This dataset gives researchers a starting point for building detectors against this kind of misuse. The synthetic images are not clinically valid and must not be used for diagnosis.

name: Multi-Class Vehicle Detection Dataset for Dense and Heterogeneous Urban Traffic in Bangladesh
description: This dataset addresses a gap in vehicle detection research by providing a street-level image corpus of heterogeneous urban traffic with regional vehicle types absent from established driving benchmarks. It contains 6,989 manually annotated images captured by the authors at various points in Sylhet, Bangladesh, between August and December 2025, enabling researchers to develop and benchmark multi-class vehicle detection models using deep learning and computer vision under real-world traffic and imaging variability. Data Collection Sources and Scope Data was collected at street level under real road conditions: Sources: Smartphone photography by the authors using high-resolution mobile devices in Sylhet, Bangladesh. Collection period: August 2025 to December 2025. Final released volume: 6,989 images. Frames without a target vehicle class were removed during collection, so every image contains at least one annotated instance. Illumination coverage: Each image carries one illumination label assigned by visual inspection: 3,350 day and 3,639 night, a near-balanced split across lighting conditions. Processing: No augmentation, resizing, or colour correction was applied, so the images retain natural variability in brightness, contrast, sharpness, and overall quality from real-world imaging environments. Ethics: No personal information was accessed, recorded, or disclosed at any stage of the study; all images were fully anonymised prior to dataset creation to ensure confidentiality and ethical compliance. Class Definitions: The dataset includes eleven vehicle classes: i. Bicycle ii. Bike iii. Bus iv. CNGRickshaw v. Car vi. CycleRickshaw vii. Leguna viii. Microbus ix. Pickup x. Truck xi. VanRickshaw The taxonomy includes regional types — motorised three-wheeler CNG rickshaws, cycle rickshaws, van rickshaws, and Legunas — absent from benchmarks such as KITTI, Cityscapes, BDD100K, and COCO. Key Features: Regional vehicle types absent from established driving benchmarks Near-balanced split across day and night lighting conditions Exhaustive, non-overlapping manual annotation across all eleven classes Unedited images retaining natural real-world imaging variability Visually similar three-wheeler body types within a single taxonomy Use Cases: i. Multi-class vehicle detection with deep learning and computer vision ii. Traffic image analysis iii. Detection under low illumination iv. Long-tailed and few-shot detection v. Fine-grained discrimination between visually similar three-wheeler body types vi. Evaluating detector robustness and generalisation under real-world conditions File Format JPG images at 1280 × 720, with one plain-text annotation file per image in the Ultralytics YOLO convention. Annotations are axis-aligned bounding boxes produced manually in Roboflow, with coordinates normalised to the image dimensions so they remain valid after rescaling. Each image also carries one illumination label (day or night).

name: A Multi-Patient Brain CT Dataset for Edge-AI-Enabled Intracranial Hemorrhage Detection on Raspberry Pi
description: This dataset comprises 852 multi-angle brain Computed Tomography (CT) scan images collected across multiple patients presenting with intracranial hemorrhage (ICH), structured to support rapid computer-aided diagnosis and edge computing research. All images are standardized in PNG format and indexed by individual patient cases (e.g., sequential cross-sectional slices per patient) to facilitate robust, patient-level train-validation-test partitioning without data leakage. Bounding-box annotations are provided in standard YOLO format to enable direct training, evaluation, and deployment of lightweight object detection architectures—specifically the nano variants of YOLO—on resource-constrained single-board computers such as the Raspberry Pi. The dataset is fully anonymized, with all Protected Health Information (PHI) and DICOM metadata removed, providing a reliable benchmark for developing low-latency Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) screening tools, mobile triage systems, and automated point-of-care neuroimaging diagnostics in resource-limited clinical environments.

name: PatchCamelyon (PCam): Histopathology Patch Classification Benchmark
description: PatchCamelyon (PCam) is a widely utilized benchmark dataset designed for machine learning research in digital histopathology without the compute overhead of gigapixel whole-slide processing. Derived from the CAMELYON16 sentinel lymph node dataset, PCam consists of 327,680 color image patches (96x96 pixels at 10x equivalent magnification) split into standardized training (262,144), validation (32,768), and testing (32,768) sets. A patch is labeled positive (binary 1) if its central 32x32 pixel region contains at least one pixel of tumor tissue, while excluding ambiguous borderline cases. PCam is balanced across classes and serves as an accessible testbed for rotation equivariance, self-supervised learning, and convolutional neural network development.

name: Raw and Preprocessed EEG of ILS-Screened Verbal–Visual and Active–Reflective Learners during the Short Hagen Matrices Test (HMT-S)
description: This dataset contains 8-channel electroencephalography (EEG) recordings of 28 Indonesian undergraduate students labelled on two Felder–Silverman learning-style dimensions: Verbal–Visual (7 Verbal, 7 Visual) and Active–Reflective (7 Active, 7 Reflective). Participants were screened with an Indonesian translation of the Index of Learning Styles (ILS), and only those with a moderate-to-strong preference (score ≥ 5) on the target dimension were recorded. During recording, participants solved the six items of the short form of the Hagen Matrices Test (HMT-S). Each item was shown for 15 s without and then for 15 s with its answer options (12 stimuli, about 3 min of task EEG). EEG was acquired at 250 Hz with an OpenBCI Cyton board from Fp1, Fp2, F3, F4, C3, C4, O1 and O2 (10–20 system). The data are organized in two tiers: (1) Raw EEG (OpenBCI GUI export, CSV) with the answer log of each participant (XLSX), recording the selected option, the correct option and the time of each answer; (2) Band-pass filtered (8–30 Hz) EEG segmented into non-overlapping 1-s, 250-sample windows aligned to the task phases (CSV; 180 windows × 8 channels per participant). The data can be used for subject-independent classification of learning-style preferences, comparison of filtering, artifact-handling and feature-extraction methods, deep learning on EEG, and analyses relating EEG to task performance. The README file describes every folder, file and column, as well as the known limitations of the data. The files contain no names or other direct personal identifiers.

name: Shongbad Chitro: A Multimodal Bangla News Image-Text Dataset
description: Shongbad Chitro: A Multimodal Bangla News Image-Text Dataset contains 50,000 Bangla news articles and 50,000 associated image files. It supports research in Bangla natural language processing, computer vision, and multimodal learning. The recorded publication dates range from 13 August 2023 to 30 August 2026. The articles are organized into nine major categories: বাংলাদেশ (Bangladesh), রাজনীতি (Politics), বিশ্ব (World), বাণিজ্য (Business), মতামত (Opinion), খেলা (Sports), বিনোদন (Entertainment), চাকরি (Jobs), and জীবনযাপন (Lifestyle). The dataset preserves 113 original subcategory labels, providing a two-level structure for broad and detailed news classification. Each article record includes its title, body text, subcategory, major category, publication date, source URL, author, image caption where available, image URL, and local image path. These fields connect textual content with associated images and source information. Major categories were assigned using the source sections recorded in article URLs, supplemented by custom mappings for topics outside the nine-category structure. Education is grouped under Bangladesh, literature under Entertainment, religion and general science and technology under Lifestyle, and freelancing under Jobs. A Category Mapping worksheet documents these groupings and their article counts. The dataset is distributed as an Excel workbook and an images folder. The workbook contains article records, summary statistics, and category mappings. It also retains 86 empty trailing rows, which are excluded from the total of 50,000 articles. Shongbad Chitro can support research on Bangla news classification, hierarchical classification, multimodal topic prediction, image–text retrieval, image captioning, and news summarization.

description: The Sleep-EDF Database Expanded contains 197 whole-night polysomnographic (PSG) recordings hosted on PhysioNet. name: Small and Fast Falling object LiDAR and RGB Dataset
description: This dataset supports the Feature-Fused Three-Frame (FF3F) framework for detecting and tracking small, fast-moving objects using LiDAR. It contains 480 Intel RealSense L515 recordings, divided into training, validation and test sets of 160 recordings each. Each set includes 40 recordings of vertical free fall, rolling-to-edge fall, bounce/rebound and cluttered-background free fall. The release includes depth recordings, timestamps, camera parameters, background measurements, manually annotated bounding boxes and visibility states, source code, trained models, calibration mappings and evaluation results. It supports reproduction of tracking, motion-estimation, component-ablation and confidence-calibration results, together with validation-recording alert replay. Three-dimensional reference positions are derived from the annotations and the same LiDAR measurements, rather than independent motion measurements. Alert timing represents timestamp-paced replay, not live warning delivery. RGB recordings were recorded but not used in these experiments and are excluded from this release.

name: A dataset for soybean yield prediction (Machine Learning applications)
description: The dataset combines meteorological, soil and soybean yield data collected from three publicly available sources: the Brazilian National Institute of Meteorology (Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia - INMET), the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística - IBGE), and the International Soil Reference and Information Centre (ISRIC). The final dataset consists of 765 observations and 37 variables. Each observation corresponds to a municipality-harvest instance and is associated with the soybean yield observed at the end of the growing season. Meteorological variables were derived from hourly measurements collected by INMET and aggregated using simple averages over the period from October 10 to December 31, lacking two-months for the harvest in February (the growing cycle of soybean was assumed as approximately 125 days). This two-month forecasting horizon has been adopted in previous crop yield prediction studies using Machine Learning applications. Soil variables were collected at the municipality level and used as static features, while additional engineered variables were extracted from the raw meteorological data.

name: A Sri Lankan dataset of Tibial shaft X-ray images for fracture detection and classification
description: This dataset includes tibial shaft X-rays collected from Ashraf Memorial Hospital, Kalmunai. This dataset can be used for tasks like object detection, image analysis, fracture classification, and segmentation. The X-ray images were organized into 2 folders, which are annotated data and raw data. The X-ray images are further organized into annotated and raw data. The annotated dataset contains 253 fractured tibial shaft X-ray images, with fracture regions annotated for object detection. The raw data include 244 non-fractured tibial shaft X-ray images collected from 204 patients, together with the corresponding raw images of the annotated fractured cases. All the images are in .jpg, .png or .jpeg format. The annotated images and associated annotations can be used for fracture-region localization and object detection, while the classified fractured and non-fractured images can be used for binary fracture classification and related medical image analysis tasks. The fractured data is split into training and testing sets in a 70:30 ratio. Dataset collection: • Source: Ashraf Memorial Hospital, Kalmunai • Capture Method: Collected from PACS (Picture Archiving and Communication System) and using a phone camera. • Anonymization: All data were rigorously anonymized to maintain confidentiality and privacy. Dataset composition: • Total Participants: 438 patients, totalling 497 images. Anterior-Posterior (AP) and Lateral (L) views were obtained from both male and female patients aged between 18 and 65 years. Variables: • Fragmentary segmental fracture: 17 • Fragmented wedge fracture: 22 • Intact segmental fracture:7 • Intact wedge fracture: 74 • Oblique fracture: 38 • Spiral fracture: 30 • Transverse fracture: 65 • Non-fracture: 244

name: A Synchronized Chittagonian Speech Corpus for Dialect ASR and Speech Translation
description: This dataset presents a synchronized Chittagonian speech corpus developed for low-resource speech processing and dialect translation. The corpus contains 8,004 Chittagonian speech samples paired with corresponding Chittagonian transcripts and Standard Bangla translations. The textual component of the dataset is taken from the publicly available Kothon dataset, a Chittagonian–Standard Bangla parallel text resource. In this work, the original text pairs were extended with newly collected speech recordings from native Chittagonian speakers, creating a synchronized speech-text corpus for automatic speech recognition (ASR), speech-to-speech translation, machine translation, dialect normalization, and text-to-speech (TTS) . The dataset is organized into predefined training, validation, and test splits containing 6,403, 801, and 800 samples, respectively. Each audio recording is provided in WAV format. This resource aims to support reproducible research on Chittagonian, an under-resourced regional variety of Bangla, by enabling the development and evaluation of machine learning models for dialect-aware speech and language technologies.

name: UIA-IOT-IDS dataset: Comprehensive IoT network intrusion detection and sensor-anomaly
description: This record contains two complementary, fully labelled datasets for machine-learning-based IoT security, together with the complete acquisition and analysis code. All data were collected from a single physical smart-home testbed at the University of Agder (Grimstad, Norway), built around a resource-constrained Raspberry Pi 3 gateway, five ESP8266 + DHT22 temperature/humidity nodes in distinct rooms, a PySense board, a Flask IoT server with InfluxDB storage, and three Kali Linux attacker VMs. Network flows were computed on-device in real time by a custom tcpdump-based extractor, so no raw PCAP is stored. The deposit is organised into two datasets that serve two tasks: (1) IDS_Dataset - network-flow INTRUSION DETECTION. The "Original" folder holds the raw, as-collected flows: 3,637,408 labelled bidirectional records across 54 classes, each described by 75 columns (6 identifier/metadata fields + 69 statistical features) plus a label. Of the 69 features, 46 are schema-compatible with CIC-IoT-2023 and 23 are additional bidirectional descriptors (per-direction packet counts, packet-length and inter-arrival-time statistics, and flow rates). The "Balanced" folder holds a cleaned, SMOTE-balanced version: 1,415,074 records, one CSV per class, with identifier and zero-variance columns removed (64 features + label). The taxonomy spans 51 attack sub-types in nine categories - Reconnaissance, DoS, DDoS, Brute Force, Web-based, Mirai, Spoofing, False Data Injection and Backdoor/C2 - plus three benign traffic types (sensor, SSH, Grafana). It reproduces the eight CIC-IoT-2023 categories and adds families absent from common benchmarks: False Data Injection (direct injection and man-in-the-middle sensor replay) and Backdoor/command-and-control beaconing. (2) AD_Dataset - sensor ANOMALY DETECTION. The "Benign" folder holds timestamped temperature and humidity readings from the five DHT22 nodes (one CSV per node); the "Abnormal" folder holds readings from three anomaly sources: a heat-biased PySense board (hardware fault), direct false-data injection, and ARP-spoofing replay. 4,253,024 readings fall within the 1 March - 13 April 2026 window analysed in the article; earlier readings are also included. Each reading is stored as one row carrying either a temperature or a humidity value (InfluxDB export format). All tabular data are UTF-8 CSV files with a header row; every network-flow record carries an explicit label. The deposit also includes the full code: the real-time flow extractor, the Flask server with intentionally vulnerable endpoints, the attack and injection scripts, the SMOTE preprocessing, and the model code (XGBoost benchmark, LSTM-autoencoder, MAML, Prototypical Networks). A disjoint base/novel class split supports supervised, unsupervised and few-shot detection research.

name: UzSER-MFCC
description: This dataset provides acoustic features for speech emotion recognition (SER) in Uzbek, a low-resource Turkic language. It is derived from 598 emotional speech utterances (26.5 min in total; 0.41–4.99 s, mean 2.66 s) segmented from the dialogue of three Uzbek-language feature films (Novda, Tinchlik ortida, Vasiyat) publicly available on YouTube. The utterances were spoken by approximately 12–13 speakers (about 4 female and 8–9 male) and were labelled by four annotators into six emotion classes: anger (ANG, 101), disgust (DIS, 108), fear (FEA, 106), happiness (HAP, 73), neutral (NEU, 106) and sadness (SAD, 104). Source audio was decoded with FFmpeg and standardised to 16 kHz, 16-bit, mono PCM before feature extraction. Because the source films are protected by copyright, raw audio is not distributed. Instead, the dataset contains: (1) metadata.csv – one row per utterance with emotion label, source film, duration and signal-quality measures; (2) features/utterance_mfcc40_stats.csv – 400 utterance-level statistics computed from 40 MFCCs and their first- and second-order derivatives; (3) features/frame_mfcc13/ – frame-level 13-dimensional MFCC matrices (NumPy .npy, 25 ms Hamming window, 10 ms hop) for every utterance; (4) tables/ and figures/ – descriptive statistics, class distributions and baseline results; (5) scripts/ – the complete Python code for feature extraction, statistics, figures and baseline classification. Baseline stratified 5-fold cross-validation on the utterance-level features gives 45.8% accuracy (UAR 0.449) for an SVM and 47.0% accuracy (UAR 0.462) for a random forest, against a chance level of 16.7%. The emotions are unevenly distributed across the three films, so film-aware evaluation is recommended (see README.md). The dataset can be used for benchmarking SER methods, cross-lingual and transfer-learning experiments, and feature-level research for Uzbek.

description: VegHealth14 is a leaf image dataset for classifying the health condition of 14 vegetables that are widely grown in Bangladesh: bean, bitter gourd, bottle gourd, cabbage, cauliflower, chilli, cucumber, eggplant, okra, potato, radish, ridge gourd, snake gourd and tomato. It contains 53 classes. Each crop has one healthy class and between two and six classes of disease or pest damage. The conditions include fungal diseases (downy mildew, anthracnose, Alternaria spot, leaf mold, late blight), bacterial diseases (bacterial spot, bacterial wilt, black rot), viral diseases (mosaic virus, leaf curl virus, yellow leaf curl virus) and damage from jassids, leaf-eating insects, insect egg masses and mites. The images were gathered from several publicly available open-source datasets and combined into a single collection with a consistent class structure. The source images came in many sizes, from 128×128 to 6000×4000 pixels, and in JPEG, PNG, and WebP formats. Preprocessing 1. Files in each class folder were renamed to sequential numbers (1.jpg, 2.jpg, 3.jpg and so on). 2. Every image was resized to two standard resolutions, 224×224 and 512×512 pixels. Images were scaled directly to a square without cropping or padding, so the whole leaf stays in the frame, but non-square photos are slightly stretched. 3. All images were converted to RGB JPEG (8-bit, quality 95). PNG and WebP files were converted to JPEG. 4. Exact duplicate images were identified by MD5 hash. Some source datasets already contained oversampled copies, so the combined collection includes 11,421 files that duplicate another image in the same class and 157 images that appear in two classes. Some source images were smaller than the target size and had to be enlarged: Cabbage (150×150), Snake Gourd (128×128 to 224×224), Potato and some Tomato and Cauliflower images (256×256). These look softer than the rest, especially at 512×512. Augmentation The augmented versions balance the dataset to exactly 1,000 images per class. Only unique images were used as the base for augmentation: exact duplicates within a class were removed first, and images found in more than one class were excluded. Two classes had more than 1,000 unique images (Eggplant Healthy and Eggplant Mosaic Virus Disease), so 1,000 were randomly selected (seed 42). The two Potato blight classes already had exactly 1,000 and were not augmented. For every other class, augmented images were added until the class reached 1,000. The following techniques were used, alone or in combination: Rotation: 90°, 180° or 270° clockwise Flipping: horizontal or vertical Centre zoom crop: the central 90% or 80% of the image, resized back to full size Corner zoom crop: the top-left, top-right, bottom-left or bottom-right 85% of the image, resized back to full size Total image before augmentation: 27,282 Total image after augmentation: 53000

name: A Visual and Thermal Imaging Dataset of Lemon Fruits Following Controlled Hot-Water Treatment
description: This dataset contains visual and thermal image data collected from 140 lemon fruits (Citrus limon) to investigate surface appearance and thermal responses following controlled hot-water treatment. which was maintained consistently across all image files and processing outputs. The specific cultivar of the lemons was not independently verified. It has been developed and annotated in College of Engineering, Nanjing Agricultural University, Nanjing 210031, China, For each lemon, two visual images were acquired from operationally designated V and H views using the main rear camera of an iPhone 16 Pro Max (48 MP; f/1.78). The smartphone was mounted on a tripod at a fixed distance of 18 cm from the fruit. The lemon was placed on printed blue-grid graph paper, with major grid lines spaced 1.0 cm apart to provide a spatial reference. The fruit was repositioned between acquisitions to obtain the second view. the views are designated operationally as V and H rather than being assumed to be perfectly orthogonal. Thermal images were acquired before and after a controlled hot-water treatment. An initial thermal image (T₀) was recorded before treatment. Each lemon was then fully submerged individually in boiling water maintained at approximately °C for 60 s using a mesh holder. After removal from the water, the fruit was blotted dry using a consistent procedure. Thermal images were acquired using a UNI-T UTi165A handheld infrared thermal imager (160 × 120 pixels; NETD: 50 mK; stated accuracy: ±2 °C or ±2%). The thermal camera was mounted at a fixed distance of 15 cm, with emissivity set to 0.95 and the rainbow colour palette selected. Five additional thermal images were recorded immediately after treatment (T₁) and at 1, 2, 3, and 4 min after treatment (T₂–T₅). The dataset consists exclusively of image data and includes multiple representations of the acquired visual and thermal images. These include: - Raw visual images from the V and H views. - Segmented visual images containing the isolated lemon regions. - Corresponding visual image masks. - Raw thermal images acquired at six time points (T₀–T₅). - Thermal images preserved in TIFF format. - Segmented thermal images containing the isolated lemon regions. - Corresponding thermal image masks. In total, 1,120 primary images were acquired from the 140 lemons, comprising 280 visual images (two views per lemon) and 840 thermal images (six time points per lemon). Additional segmented images, masks, and TIFF-format files are provided as processed or preserved versions of the corresponding primary image data. where applicable, view and thermal time-point labels. Sample inclusion or exclusion was based solely on image quality and was independent of any external target or measurement values. The dataset is intended to provide traceable raw and processed visual and thermal image data for lemon imaging, segmentation, thermal-response analysis, and related computer vision or machine learning research.

name: WeedVision-14: A Field-Scale Image Dataset for Multi-Species Weed Detection and Segmentation Task
description: WeedVision-14 is a multi-format labeled image dataset comprising 10,461 RGB images of 14 weed species commonly found in major cereal cropping systems of the Indo-Gangetic Plain, India. The images were collected at the experimental research field of ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI), New Delhi (28°38′N, 77°09′E), under natural field conditions during the cropping season, with variations in illumination, background, viewing angle, camera distance, and weed growth conditions. After field collection, the images were pre-processed and standardized to a uniform resolution of 512 × 512 pixels. The dataset covers major weed types, including narrow-leaf (grass) weeds (Bermuda Grass and Crowfoot Grass), sedge weed (Rice Sedge), and broadleaf weeds (Green Amaranth, Lamb's Quarters, Nettle-leaved Goosefoot, Benghal Dayflower, Field Bindweed, Lesser Swine Cress, Common Mallow, Burclover, Congress Grass, Stonebreaker, and Horse Purslane). The dataset supports core computer vision tasks, including weed classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. The dataset was labeled under expert supervision, with bounding-box annotations and pixel-level segmentation masks generated to support weed detection and segmentation, respectively. The bounding-box annotations define the spatial extent of individual weed plants and are provided in YOLO, Pascal VOC, and COCO formats, while the segmentation masks represent the corresponding weed regions at the pixel level and are provided as binary and multiclass masks. The dataset contains 16,079 detection instances and 20,414 segmentation mask instances across all 14 weed classes. WeedVision-14 provides a standardized resource for developing and evaluating computer vision models for automated weed identification, detection, and segmentation.

name: YemSarc: A Multimodal Benchmark Dataset for Sarcasm Detection in Yemeni and Related Arabic Dialects
description: YemSarc is the first multimodal (text, audio, and video) benchmark dataset for sarcasm detection in Yemeni dialectal Arabic and seven additional Arabic dialects. It comprises 630 balanced utterances (315 sarcastic, 315 non-sarcastic) drawn from naturally occurring conversational exchanges across eight Arabic dialects: Mahwiti, Ibbi, Adeni, Sanaani, Dhamari, Saudi, Egyptian, and Taizzi. Each target utterance is paired with its preceding conversational context and is represented across three synchronized modalities: written transcript, audio segment, and video frame sequence. The dataset was constructed from two widely popular Yemeni comedic drama series (Bayt Al-Madaliz and Khuruj Nihai), sourced from their official YouTube channels. Annotation was carried out through a structured three-phase protocol by three expert academic linguists, achieving a final inter-annotator agreement of Fleiss' Kappa = 0.7473. The dataset is released with a fully reproducible, speaker-independent, and statistically audited evaluation pipeline. This dataset is intended for non-commercial academic research purposes, including multimodal sarcasm detection, Arabic dialectal NLP, and social media analysis. The dataset is licensed under CC BY 4.0.
